Severe Flooding Disrupts Bhutan’s Hydroelectric Power Generation and Transmission

Heavy monsoonal rains have triggered severe flooding across central and eastern Bhutan, causing extensive disruption at several hydroelectric plants and transmission corridors vital to the country’s electric utilities industry. Authorities report ongoing operational challenges as swollen rivers and landslides continue to threaten key generating sites and the high-voltage lines that supply domestic and export markets.

The Bhutanese Department of Hydropower and Power Systems (DHPS) confirmed that at least two major generating stations, the Chulompa and Tashigang Hydropower Projects, have scaled back production due to both inundated turbine halls and access difficulties for maintenance crews. “Our plants along the Drangme Chhu and Mangde Chhu rivers are experiencing unprecedented inflows,” said Dhendup Wangchuk, spokesperson for the DHPS. “Safety systems are engaged, but the risk of further equipment damage remains high as the floodwaters have not receded.”

The situation has been exacerbated by landslides blocking the East-West highway, hampering the movement of repair teams and the delivery of crucial spare parts to affected sites. Bhutan Power Transmission Corporation (BPTC), the country’s main grid operator, reported that floodwaters had toppled four transmission towers in the Sarpang district, temporarily cutting power to more than 45,000 households and several industrial customers. Emergency restoration teams are working in hazardous conditions to stabilize the grid, but continued rainfall is hampering progress.

PowerGen Bhutan, a leading independent operator, said it had activated emergency protocols at its Wangdue facility following a surge in river debris that threatened to clog intakes. “We are running at 60% of typical capacity to avoid turbine damage,” said Tsering Dorji, site manager at Wangdue. “Our priority is safety, but we are closely monitoring the situation for any escalation.”

Analysts warn that if the extreme weather persists, Bhutan may be forced to curtail electricity exports, which typically account for a significant portion of sector revenues. “With several plants offline and infrastructure fragile, the risk of cascading grid failures cannot be discounted,” said Lhendup Tshering, an energy sector analyst based in Thimphu. The Bhutan Electricity Trade Association has called for urgent government support to expedite repairs and review flood resilience measures at generation and transmission assets.

At the time of writing, meteorological authorities forecast further heavy rainfall in the coming days, heightening uncertainty for the electric utilities industry as it manages both immediate disruptions and the prospect of prolonged outage risks.
